questions.text: The Early Christian basilica established which major architectural form that would become dominant in Western religious architecture?

options.text: Centralized, domed structure with a focus on verticality and light
Rectangular hall with colonnaded aisles (basilica form)
Cruciform church with transepts and a central nave
Octagonal temple with ambulatory and radial symmetry

rationale.a: Centralized, domed structures are characteristic of Byzantine architecture, not Early Christian basilicas.
rationale.c: Cruciform churches are a later development, though some Early Christian basilicas included transepts.
rationale.d: Octagonal temples are associated with Byzantine centralized plans, not Early Christian basilicas.
rationale.correct: Early Christians (4th–5th centuries) inherited Roman basilica forms—rectangular halls with colonnaded aisles—but repurposed them as places of worship' and that the basilica became 'the dominant Early Christian and Western church form.'

questions.text: Which Byzantine structure, completed 537 CE in Constantinople, is credited to architects Anthemius of Tralles and Isidore of Miletus?

options.text: Old St. Peter's Basilica
Church of SS. Sergius and Bacchus
Hagia Sophia
San Vitale

rationale.a: Old St. Peter's Basilica (begun 326–333 CE) was an Early Christian basilica in Rome, not designed by these architects.
rationale.b: Church of SS. Sergius and Bacchus (527–536 CE) was also designed by Anthemius of Tralles but is described as a 'precursor' to Hagia Sophia with an octagonal plan.
rationale.d: San Vitale (526–547 CE) is located in Ravenna, Italy, and is not attributed to these architects.
rationale.correct: Hagia Sophia (532–537 CE) was designed by Anthemius of Tralles and Isidore of Miletus and remains 'the supreme example' of Byzantine architecture with its massive dome appearing to hover weightlessly.

questions.text: Which structural innovation, described as a 'spherical triangle,' allowed Byzantine architects to place circular domes on square bases?

options.text: Barrel vault
Groin vault
Pendentive
Flying buttress

rationale.a: A barrel vault is a continuous semicircular vault, not a structural solution for dome-on-square transitions.
rationale.b: A groin vault is the intersection of two barrel vaults; it does not address dome placement on square bases.
rationale.d: Flying buttresses are external support structures used in later Medieval architecture, not Byzantine dome solutions.
rationale.correct: The article defines the pendentive as 'a spherical triangle that transitions a square base to a circular dome opening' and calls it the 'defining innovation' of Byzantine architecture that 'created the iconic Byzantine church form.'
